claim: Sleeping Beauty transposon integrations can be biased towards endogenous Alu retrotransposons using dCas9 as a targeting domain in an sgRNA-dependent manner in human cells.
source: Here we demonstrate biased genome-wide integration of the Sleeping Beauty (SB) transposon by combining it with components of the CRISPR/Cas9 system. We provide proof-of-concept that it is possible to influence the target site selection of SB by fusing it to a catalytically inactive Cas9 (dCas9) and by providing a single guide RNA (sgRNA) against the human Alu retrotransposon.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the main finding that SB transposon integration can be biased using dCas9 and sgRNA targeting Alu elements, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Enrichment of transposon integrations was dependent on the sgRNA and occurred in an asymmetric pattern with a bias towards sites in a relatively narrow, 300 bp window downstream of the sgRNA targets.
source: Enrichment of transposon integrations was dependent on the sgRNA, and occurred in an asymmetric pattern with a bias towards sites in a relatively narrow, 300 bp window downstream of the sgRNA targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequencing data and bioinformatic analysis showing statistically significant enrichment in a 300 bp window downstream of sgRNA target sites.

claim: The targeting mechanism specified by CRISPR/Cas9 forces integration into genomic regions that are otherwise poor targets for SB transposition.
source: Our data indicate that the targeting mechanism specified by CRISPR/Cas9 forces integration into genomic regions that are otherwise poor targets for SB transposition.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that the targeted regions have lower TA dinucleotide frequency and higher nucleosome occupancy, which are normally disfavored by SB.

claim: Retroviruses have the capability of shuttling a transgene into target cells and stably integrating it into the genome, resulting in long-lasting expression.
source: These viruses have the capability of shuttling a transgene into target cells and stably integrating it into the genome, resulting in long-lasting expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about retroviral vectors cited in the context of gene delivery systems.

claim: Transposons can be developed as non-viral gene delivery tools that are simpler and cheaper to produce, handle and store than retroviral vectors.
source: Thus, transposons can be developed as non-viral gene delivery tools (Ivics et al., 2009) that are simpler and cheaper to produce, handle and store than retroviral vectors (Hudecek and Ivics, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work establishing these properties of transposon systems.

claim: The absence of viral proteins may prevent immune reactions that are observed with AAV-based vectors.
source: The absence of viral proteins may also prevent immune reactions that are observed with adeno-associated virus (AAV)-based vectors (Mingozzi and High, 2011; Hareendran et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on cited literature about immune reactions to AAV vectors.

claim: The Sleeping Beauty transposon is active across a wide range of cell types.
source: It is active across a wide range of cell types (Ivics et al., 1997; Izsvák et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating SB activity in various cell types.

claim: Hyperactive variants such as the SB100X transposase catalyze gene transfer in human cells with high efficiency.
source: hyperactive variants such as the SB100X transposase catalyze gene transfer in human cells with high efficiency (Mátés et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the study that characterized SB100X.

claim: Lentiviral or γ-retroviral vectors actively target genes or transcriptional start sites.
source: For example, lentiviral or γ-retroviral vectors actively target genes or transcriptional start sites (Schröder et al., 2002; Cohn et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2003; Cattoglio et al., 2010; Mitchell et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the integration preferences of retroviral vectors.

claim: The SB transposon displays a great deal of specificity of insertion at the primary DNA sequence level, almost exclusively integrating into TA dinucleotides.
source: In contrast, the SB transposon displays a great deal of specificity of insertion at the primary DNA sequence level – almost exclusively integrating into TA dinucleotides (Vigdal et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work characterizing SB integration specificity.

claim: SB transposon inserts randomly on a genome-wide scale.
source: but inserts randomly on a genome-wide scale (Yant et al., 2005; Moldt et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to genome-wide integration studies.

claim: The position of a transgene in the genome can have an effect on the expression of the transgene, endogenous genes or both.
source: For example, the position of a transgene in the genome can have an effect on the expression of the transgene, endogenous genes or both (Bestor, 2000; Ellis, 2005; Hacein-Bey-Abina et al., 2003; Stein et al., 2010; Howe et al., 2008; Cavazzana-Calvo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting position effects in gene therapy.

claim: Insertion of transgenes can disrupt genomic regulation, either by direct insertional mutagenesis of cellular genes or regulatory elements, or by upregulation of genes in the vicinity of the integration site.
source: Insertion of transgenes can disrupt genomic regulation, either by direct insertional mutagenesis of cellular genes or regulatory elements, or by upregulation of genes in the vicinity of the integration site.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the risks of integrating vectors, supported by the context of cited clinical cases.

claim: For CRISPR/Cas nucleases, target specificity is determined by a single guide RNA (sgRNA).
source: While for ZFNs and TALENs target specificity is determined by their amino acid sequence, Cas nucleases need to be supplied with a single guide RNA (sgRNA) that determines their target specificity (Jinek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRISPR/Cas9 mechanism, supported by citation to the foundational paper.

claim: The CRISPR/Cas system is significantly more flexible than other designer nucleases.
source: This makes the CRISPR/Cas system significantly more flexible than other designer nucleases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-guided mechanism compared to protein-based targeting of ZFNs and TALENs.

claim: A double-strand break in a target cell is usually repaired by the cell's DNA repair machinery, either via non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) or homologous recombination (HR).
source: A double-strand break (DSB) in a target cell is usually repaired by the cell's DNA repair machinery, either via non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) or homologous recombination (HR) (Mao et al., 2008; Kakarougkas and Jeggo, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA repair pathways, supported by citations.

claim: The efficiency of the HR pathway is low compared to the efficiency of the nuclease.
source: However, the efficiency of the HR pathway is low compared to the efficiency of the nuclease (Lieber, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to work on DNA repair pathway efficiency.

claim: Targeted nucleases are highly efficient at knocking out genes but less efficient at inserting DNA.
source: This bottleneck means that targeted nucleases are highly efficient at knocking out genes (Hockemeyer et al., 2009; Hockemeyer et al., 2011), but less efficient at inserting DNA (Aird et al., 2018), particularly when compared to the integrating viral and non-viral vectors mentioned previously.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies comparing knockout and knock-in efficiencies.

claim: Several transposon systems, notably the SB and the piggyBac systems have been successfully targeted to a range of exogenous or endogenous loci in the human genome.
source: Several transposon systems, notably the SB and the piggyBac systems have been successfully targeted to a range of exogenous or endogenous loci in the human genome (Voigt et al., 2012; Ammar et al., 2012; Ivics et al., 2007; reviewed in Kovač and Ivics, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous targeting studies.

claim: A consistent finding across all targeted transposition studies is that while some bias can be introduced to the vector's integration profile, the number of targeted integrations is relatively low when compared to the number of untargeted background integrations.
source: However, a consistent finding across all targeted transposition studies is that while some bias can be introduced to the vector's integration profile, the number of targeted integrations is relatively low when compared to the number of untargeted background integrations (Kovač and Ivics, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review summarizing previous targeting studies.

claim: A catalytically inactive variant of Cas9 called dCas9 has previously been used to target enzymes including transcriptional activators, repressors, base editors and others to specific target sequences.
source: A catalytically inactive variant of Cas9 called dCas9 ('dead Cas9', containing the mutations D10A and H840A), has previously been used to target enzymes including transcriptional activators (Konermann et al., 2015; Maeder et al., 2013; Perez-Pinera et al., 2013), repressors (Yeo et al., 2018; Gilbert et al., 2013), base editors (Eid et al., 2018; Gehrke et al., 2018) and others (Chaikind et al., 2016; Halperin et al., 2018) to specific target sequences.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting various applications of dCas9 fusions.

claim: Using the Hsmar1 human transposon, a 15-fold enrichment of transposon insertions into a 600 bp target region was observed in an in vitro plasmid-to-plasmid assay employing a dCas9-Hsmar1 fusion.
source: By using the Hsmar1 human transposon (Miskey et al., 2007), a 15-fold enrichment of transposon insertions into a 600 bp target region was observed in an in vitro plasmid-to-plasmid assay employing a dCas9-Hsmar1 fusion (Bhatt and Chalmers, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study using dCas9 with a different transposon system.

claim: No targeted transposition was detected with the dCas9-Hsmar1 system in bacterial cells.
source: However, no targeted transposition was detected with this system in bacterial cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the same study mentioned in the previous claim.

claim: A previous study failed to target the piggyBac transposon into the HPRT gene with CRISPR/Cas9 components in human cells.
source: A previous study failed to target the piggyBac transposon into the HPRT gene with CRISPR/Cas9 components in human cells, even though some targeting was observed with other DBDs (Luo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous targeting study.

claim: Some integrations were successfully biased to the CCR5 locus using a dCas9-piggyBac fusion.
source: However, in a recent study, some integrations were successfully biased to the CCR5 locus using a dCas9-piggyBac fusion (Hew et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study demonstrating successful targeting with dCas9-piggyBac.

claim: Two recent studies showed highly specific targeting of bacterial Tn7-like transposons by an RNA-guided mechanism, but only in bacterial cells.
source: Two additional recent studies showed highly specific targeting of bacterial Tn7-like transposons by an RNA-guided mechanism, but only in bacterial cells (Strecker et al., 2019; Klompe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to two studies on RNA-guided transposition in bacteria.

claim: N57 is an N-terminal fragment of the SB transposase encompassing the N-terminal helix-turn-helix domain with dual DNA-binding and protein dimerization functions.
source: N57 is an N-terminal fragment of the SB transposase encompassing the N-terminal helix-turn-helix domain of the SB transposase with dual DNA-binding and protein dimerization functions (Izsvák et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the study characterizing N57.

claim: Fusions of N57 with various DNA-binding domains were previously shown to direct transposition catalyzed by wild-type SB transposase to specific genomic locations.
source: Fusions of N57 with the tetracycline repressor (TetR), the E2C zinc finger domain (Beerli et al., 1998), the ZF-B zinc finger domain and the DBD of the Rep protein of AAV were previously shown to direct transposition catalyzed by wild-type SB transposase to genomically located tetracycline operator (TetO) sequences, the erbB-2 gene, endogenous human L1 retrotransposons and Rep-recognition sequences, respectively (Voigt et al., 2012; Ammar et al., 2012; Ivics et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous targeting studies using N57 fusions.

claim: Four sgRNAs were designed to target the HPRT gene, with one binding in exon 7 and three in exon 3.
source: Four sgRNAs were designed to target the HPRT gene (Figure 2A), one of them (sgHPRT-0) binding in exon 7 and three (sgHPRT-1 – sgHPRT-3) in exon 3.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design, supported by reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Three sgRNAs were designed against AluY, with the first two binding at or near the conserved A-box of the Pol III promoter and the third against the A-rich stretch that separates the two monomers.
source: Three sgRNAs were designed against AluY (Figure 2D), the first two (sgAluY-1 and sgAluY-2) binding at or near the conserved A-box of the Pol III promoter that drives Alu transcription and the third (sgHPRT-3) against the A-rich stretch that separates the two monomers in the full-length Alu element.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design, supported by reference to Figure 2D.

claim: sgHPRT-0 and sgHPRT-1 resulted in strong, significant increases in HPRT disruption levels (p≤0.001).
source: Two sgRNAs (sgHPRT-0, sgHPRT-1) resulted in strong, significant increases in disruption levels (p≤0.001)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the 6-TG resistance assay with statistical analysis.

claim: sgHPRT-2 failed to increase disruption over the background level.
source: while sgHPRT-2 failed to increase disruption over the background level
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the 6-TG resistance assay.

claim: sgHPRT-3 induced weak but significant disruption (p≤0.05).
source: and sgHPRT-3 induced weak but significant disruption (p≤0.05). (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the 6-TG resistance assay with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: sgHPRT-0 yielded a total editing efficiency of 57.1% as measured by TIDE assay.
source: As measured by TIDE, sgHPRT-0 yielded a total editing efficiency of 57.1% (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the TIDE assay, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Incubation of human genomic DNA with purified Cas9 protein and in vitro transcribed sgRNAs showed detectable fragmentation of gDNA for sgAluY-1 and sgAluY-2.
source: Incubation of human genomic DNA (gDNA) with purified Cas9 protein and in vitro transcribed sgRNAs showed detectable fragmentation of gDNA for sgAluY-1 and sgAluY-2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the in vitro cleavage assay, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Twelve of 32 sequenced genomic junctions from Cas9-digested gDNA could be mapped to the AluY sequence upstream of the cleavage site and 19 could be mapped to the sequence immediately downstream.
source: Twelve of 32 sequenced genomic junctions could be mapped to the AluY sequence upstream of the cleavage site and 19 could be mapped to the sequence immediately downstream (as defined by the direction of Alu transcription).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data from cloned genomic DNA fragments.

claim: A consensus sequence generated by aligning the sequenced junctions showed significant similarity to the AluY consensus sequence, demonstrating that the DNA fragmentation was the result of Cas9-mediated cleavage.
source: A consensus sequence generated by aligning the 12 or 19 sequences showed significant similarity to the AluY consensus sequence (Figure 2F), demonstrating that the DNA fragmentation was indeed the result of Cas9-mediated cleavage.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Mismatches within the sgRNA binding sequence are tolerated to some extent, while the conserved GG dinucleotide of the NGG PAM motif did not show any sequence variation.
source: The sequence composition also revealed that mismatches within the sgRNA binding sequence are tolerated to some extent, while the conserved GG dinucleotide of the NGG PAM motif did not show any sequence variation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Three different targeting constructs were generated: a direct fusion of dCas9 with SB100X, and two adapter proteins with N57 at the C-terminus or N-terminus of dCas9.
source: For the direct fusion, the entire coding sequence of SB100X, a hyperactive version of the SB transposase (Mátés et al., 2009), was inserted at the C-terminus of the dCas9 sequence (Figure 3A, top). We only made an N-terminal SB fusion, because C-terminal tagging of the transposase enzyme completely abolishes its activity (Yant et al., 2007; Ivics et al., 2007; Wilson et al., 2005). For adapter proteins, the N57 domain was inserted at the C-terminus as well as at the N-terminus of dCas9 (Figure 3A, middle and bottom, respectively).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design with citations supporting the rationale for construct design.

claim: C-terminal tagging of the SB transposase enzyme completely abolishes its activity.
source: We only made an N-terminal SB fusion, because C-terminal tagging of the transposase enzyme completely abolishes its activity (Yant et al., 2007; Ivics et al., 2007; Wilson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing SB transposase tagging effects.

claim: Western blots using an antibody against the SB transposase verified the integrity and the expression of the fusion proteins.
source: Western blots using an antibody against the SB transposase verified the integrity and the expression of the fusion proteins (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The fusion construct dCas9-SB100X was approximately 30% as active as unfused SB100X.
source: We found that the fusion construct dCas9-SB100X was approximately 30% as active as unfused SB100X.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the transposition assay comparing colony numbers.

claim: Binding could be detected for the dCas9-N57 fusion, but not for N57-dCas9 in EMSA experiments.
source: Binding could be detected for the dCas9-N57 fusion, but not for N57-dCas9.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the EMSA shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The N57-dCas9 construct was excluded from subsequent experiments due to lack of DNA-binding activity.
source: For this reason, the N57-dCas9 construct was excluded from the subsequent experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on the EMSA results.

claim: The cleavage efficiencies of both Cas9-SB100X and Cas9-N57 were ~30% of unfused Cas9 in the presence of sgHPRT-0.
source: The cleavage efficiencies of both Cas9-SB100X and Cas9-N57 were ~30% of unfused Cas9 in the presence of sgHPRT-0 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the 6-TG resistance assay shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Binding of the Cas9 domain to its target DNA is a prerequisite for DNA cleavage.
source: Because binding of the Cas9 domain to its target DNA is a prerequisite for DNA cleavage, we infer that cleavage-competent fusion proteins are also able to bind to target DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Cas9 mechanism used to make an inference about the fusion proteins.

claim: No insertion was recovered within 5 kb in either direction from the sgHPRT-0 binding site in the HPRT locus.
source: For the HPRT locus, no insertion was recovered within 5 kb in either direction from the sgHPRT-0 binding site in our dataset (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the integration site sequencing data.

claim: Either targeting of the HPRT single-copy locus was not possible with the current system, or the number of insertion sites recovered was too low to provide the necessary resolution for detecting an effect.
source: We conclude that either targeting of this single-copy locus was not possible with the current system, or that the number of insertion sites recovered (<1000 insertions) was too low to provide the necessary resolution for detecting an effect.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for the negative result at the HPRT locus.

claim: The sgAluY-1 sgRNA has a total of 299339 target sites in the human genome (hg38).
source: The sgAluY-1 sgRNA has a total of 299339 target sites in the human genome (hg38) (the number of sites exceeds the number of AluY elements due to high conservation, and therefore presence in other Alu subfamilies).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the human genome sequence.

claim: Some enrichment (ca. 15%) was found for dCas9-N57 + SB100X in a window of 200 bp around the target sites, although not statistically significant.
source: We found some enrichment (ca. 15%) for dCas9-N57 + SB100X in a window of 200 bp around the target sites and dCas9-SB100X insertions are slightly enriched in a window of 500 bp (ca. 20%) (Figure 5C), although neither change was statistically significant.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration site data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: dCas9-SB100X insertions are slightly enriched in a window of 500 bp (ca. 20%), although not statistically significant.
source: We found some enrichment (ca. 15%) for dCas9-N57 + SB100X in a window of 200 bp around the target sites and dCas9-SB100X insertions are slightly enriched in a window of 500 bp (ca. 20%) (Figure 5C), although neither change was statistically significant.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration site data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: With dCas9-SB100X, statistically significant enrichment was detected in the insertion frequencies in a window spanning a 300 bp region downstream of the sgRNA target sites (~1.5 fold enrichment, p=0.019).
source: However, with dCas9-SB100X, we found that the enrichment occurred almost exclusively downstream of the target sites, within the AluY element. We detected statistically significant enrichment in the insertion frequencies in a window spanning a 300 bp region downstream of the sgRNA target sites (~1.5 fold enrichment, p=0.019) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is the main positive result, supported by statistical analysis of integration site data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Enrichment was also detected near target loci similar to the target site (with one mismatch), although not statistically significant.
source: We also detected enrichment near target loci similar to the target site (with one mismatch), although not statistically significant (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration sites near imperfect target matches, shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The specificity of dCas9 binding is lower than that of Cas9 cleavage.
source: This result is in agreement with the finding that the specificity of dCas9 binding is lower than that of Cas9 cleavage (Jiang and Doudna, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work characterizing dCas9 specificity.

claim: The SB insertion machinery generally disfavors loci downstream of the sgAluY-1 binding sequences.
source: Intriguingly, plotting the overall insertion frequencies around the target sites revealed that the SB insertion machinery generally disfavors loci downstream of the sgAluY-1 binding sequences (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of insertion frequency distributions shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The TA dinucleotide frequency in the targeted region is lower than in the neighboring segments.
source: To our surprise, we found that the TA dinucleotide frequency in the targeted region is in fact lower than in the neighboring segments (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The integrations within the Alu sequences are enforced to take place at TA sequences that only weakly match the preferred ATATATAT consensus palindrome.
source: Along these findings, comparison of the nucleotide composition of the targeted vs non-targeted insertion sites revealed that the integrations within the Alu sequences are enforced to take place at TA sequences that only weakly match the preferred ATATATAT consensus palindrome (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence logo analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Targeting occurs into DNA that is per se disfavored by the SB transposition machinery.
source: Thus, targeting occurs into DNA that is per se disfavored by the SB transposition machinery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TA frequency and sequence composition data.

claim: Nucleosome positioning in the genome is primarily driven by sequence.
source: Since the nucleotide composition of the targeted regions is remarkably different from that of the neighboring sequences and given that nucleosome positioning in the genome is primarily driven by sequence (Segal et al., 2006), we next investigated nucleosome occupancy of the target DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SB disfavors integrating into nucleosomal DNA.
source: This analysis recapitulated our previous finding showing that SB disfavors integrating into nucleosomal DNA (Gogol-Döring et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by the current analysis.

claim: AluY sequences are conserved regions for nucleosome formation.
source: Additionally, in agreement with previous findings of others (Englander and Howard, 1995; Tanaka et al., 2010), we found that these AluY sequences are conserved regions for nucleosome formation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by nucleosome occupancy predictions shown in Figure 6C and citations to previous studies.

claim: The observed enrichment of insertions next to sgRNA-targeted sites is likely an underestimate of the true efficiency of transposon targeting because the PCR procedure cannot detect independent targeting events that occurred at the same TA dinucleotide.
source: We consider it likely that the observed enrichment of insertions next to sgRNA-targeted sites is an underestimate of the true efficiency of transposon targeting in our experiments, because our PCR procedure followed by next generation sequencing and bioinformatic analysis cannot detect independent targeting events that had occurred at the same TA dinucleotide in the human genome.
evidence: This is speculation about a technical limitation of the methodology.

claim: The enrichment by dCas9-SB100X occurred in a relatively narrow window in the vicinity of the sites specified by the sgRNA, consistent with physical docking of the transpositional complex at the targeted sites.
source: While enrichment observed with dCas9-N57 was very weak and not statistically significant, the enrichment by dCas9-SB100X was more pronounced, and occurred in a relatively narrow window in the vicinity of the sites specified by the sgRNA. This observation is consistent with physical docking of the transpositional complex at the targeted sites, and suggests that binding of dCas9 to its target sequence and integration by the SB transposase occur within a short timeframe.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial distribution of targeted insertions.

claim: Binding of dCas9 to its target sequence and integration by the SB transposase occur within a short timeframe.
source: This observation is consistent with physical docking of the transpositional complex at the targeted sites, and suggests that binding of dCas9 to its target sequence and integration by the SB transposase occur within a short timeframe.
evidence: This is an inference based on the narrow window of enrichment.

claim: Asymmetric distributions of targeted insertions have been previously found in a study using the ISY100 transposon in combination with the ZF domain Zif268 in E. coli.
source: Asymmetric distributions of targeted insertions have been previously found in a study using the ISY100 transposon (which, like SB, is a member of the Tc1/mariner transposon superfamily) in combination with the ZF domain Zif268 in E. coli (Feng et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study showing asymmetric targeting.

claim: Asymmetric distributions of targeted insertions were found in experiments with dCas9-Hsmar1 fusions in vitro.
source: and in experiments with dCas9-Hsmar1 fusions in vitro (Bhatt and Chalmers, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Domains fused to the C-terminus of Cas9 are expected to be localized closer to the 5'-end of the target strand, or upstream of the sgRNA binding site.
source: Enrichment mainly occurring downstream of the sgRNA target site in our experiments was somewhat surprising, as domains fused to the C-terminus of Cas9 are expected to be localized closer to the 5'-end of the target strand (Oakes et al., 2014), or upstream of the sgRNA binding site.
evidence: This is based on citation to structural studies of Cas9.

claim: The fact that SB100X is connected with dCas9 by a relatively long, flexible linker could explain why enrichment can occur on the other side of the sgRNA binding site.
source: The fact that SB100X is connected with dCas9 by a relatively long, flexible linker could explain why enrichment can occur on the other side of the sgRNA binding site, but it does not explain why enrichment on the 'far side' seems to be more efficient.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of asymmetric targeting.

claim: The targeting effect in the downstream window may be more pronounced than on the other side of the sgRNA target site because there are fewer background insertions obscuring a targeting effect.
source: It is possible that the targeting effect in this window is more pronounced than on the other side of the sgRNA target site because there are fewer background insertions obscuring a targeting effect.
evidence: This is speculation about why asymmetric enrichment is observed.

claim: Addition of a large protein (dCas9 is 158 kDa) to the N-terminus of N57 may mask its function to some extent.
source: We speculate that addition of a large protein (dCas9 is 158 kDa) to the N-terminus of a relatively small polypeptide of 57 amino acids masks its function to some extent.
evidence: This is speculation about why dCas9-N57 showed minimal targeting effect.

claim: TetR, the ZF-B protein and Rep DBD that were used previously with success in conjunction with N57 are all far smaller than dCas9.
source: Indeed, TetR, the ZF-B protein and Rep DBD that were used previously with success in conjunction with N57 are all far smaller than dCas9.
evidence: This is a comparison based on known protein sizes from previous studies.

claim: The binding activity of dCas9-N57 to transposon DNA, though detectable by EMSA, may have been too weak to effectively recruit the components of the SB system to the target site.
source: The binding activity of dCas9-N57 to transposon DNA, though detectable by EMSA, may have been too weak to effectively recruit the components of the SB system to the target site.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of poor targeting with dCas9-N57.

claim: The difficulty of targeting to the HPRT gene might be associated with characteristics of the target itself or an indication that the system is not specific enough to target a single-copy site in general.
source: First, the difficulty of targeting to a single location, in this case the HPRT gene, might be associated with characteristics of the target itself or an indication that the system is not specific enough to target a single-copy site in general.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for failure to target HPRT.

claim: An integration library consisting of 21646 independent SB integrations generated by unfused SB100X without any targeting factor did not contain any integrations within 50 kb of the HPRT target sequence.
source: The fact that an integration library consisting of 21646 independent SB integrations generated by unfused SB100X without any targeting factor did not contain any integrations within 50 kb of the HPRT target sequence either (data not shown) might indicate that the HPRT gene is simply a poor target for SB integrations.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of a control integration dataset.

claim: A previous attempt to target the piggyBac transposase to the HPRT gene with CRISPR/Cas components also failed, even though targeting with other DBDs (ZFs and TALEs) was successful.
source: It should be noted that a previous attempt to target the piggyBac transposase to the HPRT gene with CRISPR/Cas components also failed, even though targeting with other DBDs (ZFs and TALEs) was successful (Luo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Both Rep-SB and Rep-N57 fusions were able to enrich SB transposon integrations in the vicinity of genomic Rep binding sites, yet they failed to target integration into the AAVS1 locus.
source: Both Rep-SB and Rep-N57 fusions were able to enrich SB transposon integrations in the vicinity of genomic Rep binding sites, yet they failed to target integration into the AAVS1 locus, the canonical integration site of AAV (Ammar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous targeting study.

claim: Selection of an appropriate target site appears to be of paramount importance for targeted transposition.
source: Thus, selection of an appropriate target site appears to be of paramount importance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the various targeting results discussed.

claim: The minimal requirements for target sites are accessibility by the transpositional complex and the presence of TA dinucleotides to support SB transposition.
source: The minimal requirements for such sites are accessibility by the transpositional complex and the presence of TA dinucleotides to support SB transposition
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of SB transposition.

claim: SB was reported to prefer insertion into TA-rich DNA in general.
